articles.text: On July 1 the Presidency of Piedmont Beautification Foundation passed from Karen Sullivan to Patty Dunlap. Sullivan completed a highly successful two years as President of the organization. Under her leadership the importance of PBF to the City of Piedmont increased significantly. Sullivan pushed the organization to increase its role from the more traditional focus on parks. Perhaps the most important undertaking was to support the construction of a new swimming pool. PBF was an early donor to the campaign to cover the shortfall in funding for this vital project. PBF followed by making the pool the focus of its efforts for 2022. It undertook a matching fund drive to raise money for the pool’s landscaping and green infrastructure. Ultimately PBF raised almost $250,000 for the pool, making it the second largest donating organization after Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization (PRFO). Other projects completed under Sullivan’s leadership included completion of beautiful new steps at the Highland/ Guildford entrance to Piedmont Park; safety bulb out landscaping; installation of water bottle filling stations; the planting of an Island Oak at the Mountain/Bellevue intersection; and the installation of a flagpole to honor the late Justice Carl Anderson. Several other projects are pending, including support for the soon to come Dearing Family Memorial and a significant upgrade of the Linda Beach Tot Lot. Throughout Sullivan’s term in office PBF’s long standing memorial bench and tree programs continued. Five memorial benches were installed, and 12 new trees were planted. PBF’s newest project is among the most exciting in recent years – the reforestation of Piedmont. Working in conjunction with Nancy Kent, the City’s Parks and Special Projects Manager (who oversaw the recently completed inventory of trees throughout the city) and incoming PBF President Patty Dunlap, a campaign to reforest the City’s trees has commenced. The initial focus is on Dracena Park, where a loss of many trees has created a huge need for replanting. The plan permits donors to direct their contributions to their own neighborhoods that need new trees. PBF involves many organizations and residents of Piedmont, all contributing to the betterment of the City. The Piedmont Garden Club was the founder of PBF and continues to pull the laboring oar. There are eight Trustees, including three appointed by the City Council (typically two Council members and the Chair of the Park Commission). The Piedmont Garden Club provides the other five Trustees, who also serve as officers. Other garden clubs represented are East Bay Garden Club, Highlanders Garden Club, and Hoe and Hope. Patty Dunlap, PBF’s newest President, will oversee the organization and its ambitious new campaign of reforestation. She is a former member of the Park Commission and served admirably as its Chair. PBF is looking forward to having her pick up the torch. Piedmont Beautification Foundation President Karen Sullivan with incoming president Patty Dunlap

articles.text: A rendering of the two main units to be built on the lot, designated as 67 Wistaria Way (left) and 77 Wistaria Way. An ADU will also be built on the property. The design was approved by the Planning Department on December 27, 2023. Neighbors of the controversial housing project at 77 Wistaria Way have recently voiced their distrust of the project’s owner-developers Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead over what they believe is an aggressive attempt to build and quickly resell a large property in the neighborhood. The story of 77 Wistaria Way begins with its original owners, Harold and Genevieve Power. Harold passed away in 1994 and Genevieve in 2020. With no children, the land was given to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Oakland to support Corpus Christi Church. Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead bought the property from the Roman Catholic Diocese on January 4, 2022. The couple, married for 10 years have lived in the Bay Area for 25 and 15 years respectively. On May 2, 2022 Geoff Gibson, Kira Mead and their daughter Mabel introduced themselves to the area by going door to door with gifts of wine and chocolates for their future neighbors. Erin Ashton, who lives nearby, recalled the event. “They were carrying a binder with information about the property next door. They showed me a rendering of their first house design, and they gave us a bottle of wine and chocolates while our daughter played with their child.” When Ashton asked if she could have a copy of the rendering to 2024 September 21, 2024 9 AM - 12 PM 800 MAGNOLIA AVE. PIEDMONT, CA RSVP: coffeecarscops@piedmont.ca.gov show her husband, they refused. “Usually when a neighbor comes to visit regarding a new project, it’s to alleviate any potential impact rather than having everything already designed,” said her husband, David Ashton. On July 11, 2022, Mead and Gibson met with the Planning Commission at its regularly scheduled public meeting for a design review. The couple requested to construct a new four-level, 4,992-square-foot single-family residence with four bedrooms, four and a half bathrooms, two offices, a recreation room, a covered entry porch, and a two-car garage. Many neighbors from surrounding properties appeared to voice their concerns about the size of the house, potential loss of scenic views and sunlight impacts on neighboring properties among others. According to the meeting minutes, their plan was rejected because “the design as submitted is too much of a high impact on the neighbors [...] The applicant should spend more time collaborating with the neighbors to get a more achievable design.” On November 14, 2022, Mead and Gibson met once again with the Planning Commission for another design review. This time, the couple requested to build a three-level, 3,699-square-foot residence with four bedrooms, four-and-a-half bathrooms, an office, and a two-car garage. Once again, many neighbors from surrounding properties appeared to voice their concerns. Gibson said that there had been multiple attempts to meet and talk with people who disapproved of the project, but that not many have come forward to further discuss issues and solutions. Commission Chair Rani Batra said that she appreciated that the couple had made changes, but that the design was still too large. Commissioner Justin Zucker was supportive of the project and voiced his concerns that a subsequent project would come back under the Housing Accountability Act. Ultimately, Gibson and Mead’s design was rejected again for many of the same reasons as in their previous design review. On April 20, 2023, Gibson and Mead submitted their application form and SB9 eligibility package to the City of Piedmont’s Planning Department. The proposed plan split the lot into two properties: one at 67 Wistaria Way, which will be 2,590 square feet, and another at 77 Wistaria Way, which would be 3,418 square feet. On August 23, 2023, lawyer Kurt Peterson sent a letter to the Planning Department on behalf of the neighbors around Wistaria Way urging the City to reject the application. The application was approved on December 27, 2023.

articles.text: Piedmont recently experienced a string of burglaries mostly targeted at residents who were on vacation for extended periods of time. On Monday, August 5, around 5:00 p.m., a residential burglary on Requa Road was reported to the police. When the residents returned home they found several items missing. An unknown suspect or suspects entered the home and stole several jewelry items including a Tiffany silver bracelet, a Tiffany silver chain bracelet and a Mikimoto bracelet. The total reported loss was $6,700. On Monday, August 5, at 11:15 p.m., a resident on Grand Avenue returned home from vacation to find his residence ransacked. The victim stated several music instruments, recording equipment and other expensive items were missing. The total value of the loss is unknown. On Thursday, August 8, a resident reported that their house on King Avenue had been burglarized the previous night. The suspect entered the home through a side window and ransacked the office and upstairs master bedroom. The total reported loss is in excess of $5,000 worth of jewelry and purses. The Piedmont Police Department encourages residents who are heading out of town to sign up for their Vacation Home Check program. Vacation Home Check is a service offered to residents who are away from their homes for a period of 4 to 30 days. If requested, members of the police department may periodically check the security of your house. If a problem is discovered, a police officer will respond and handle the situation. Residents may request this service by downloading the Vacation Home Check & Vacant Home Notification Form from the PPD’s website. The completed form may be mailed or dropped off at the Police Department at 403 Highland Avenue or emailed to vacationchecks@piedmont.ca.gov. On the form, please include important information such as who is allowed on the property while you are away, a list of pets left on the property, and the name of any caretaker(s). For more information on the Vacation Home Check program, call the police department’s non-emergency line at 420-3000.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team is back on the courts with eyes on the prize – looking to win the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division title after missing out last year. The squad opened its 2024 campaign with a scrimmage against North Coast Section foe and neighboring school College Prep on August 19. PHS went 13-8 last season and was second in the WACC to Bishop O’Dowd. They reached the D2 NCS Team Championship semifinals, falling 5-2 to eventual champions University. To reach the semis, Piedmont shutout Marin Catholic 7-0 in the first round and beat College Prep 6-1 in the quarterfinals. This year, O’Dowd still shapes up as Piedmont’s main competition for the Foothill Division title, along with Berkeley and Alameda. O’Dowd won in 2021, Piedmont claiming the crown in 2022, and O’Dowd won again last year. “O’Dowd lost their top singles starter and a couple of other girls, so it’ll still be close competition with them. Berkeley has some returners and will be a difficult team and I believe Alameda did too. But we have a good team and look even stronger in doubles,” coach Jim Landes said. Landes has his team captains for this year. Emma Eisemon is a four-year starter and a key doubles player, while Carolina Romanczuk is a three-year singles starter. “Four years down, it’s so crazy and a surreal moment. I’ve played the last three season with my partner Ceci, it’s a bit switched up this year and I’m keeping an open mind to playing doubles and even singles. I’m super excited,” Eisemon said. “Being a captain brings us a lot of responsibility. We have to be role models to the younger girls on the team and that makes me happy to try to become that role model for these girls,” Romanczuk added. Eisemon has played most of her Piedmont career with doubles partner Ceclia DeFazio, who graduated last year. Landes is taking a look at pairing her with Samantha Huynh. “This season, I don’t have any expectations and I’m playing for fun. I’m excited to see how it Staff Photos Senior Emma Eisemon was named a team captain for the upcoming season. Junior Kate Jumper is a three-year starter and a key singles player. looks, we’re moving around the lineup a lot,” Eisemon said. Romanczuk us hoping to be the team’s No. 1 singles starter, and will challenge for the position with junior Kate Jumper. Romanczuk spent time over the summer training and showing some increased power on her forehand. “At the end of last season, I sprained my ankle twice. I’ve been working hard this summer and went to a tennis academy. I’ve been working a lot and practicing,” Romanczuk said. New to the varsity roster are sophomores Emma Chan and Faith Chin, who may round out Piedmont’s doubles lineup. Piedmont gets its season started with two matches next week, at Las Lomas in Walnut Creek on Wednesday, August 28, and home on August 29 with neighbor Head Royce. articles.text: Witter Field off icially re-opened on August 14, 2024, one year after expected. A ribbon-cutting ceremony marked the apparent completion on a new track, new field drainage, and a new playing surface for football, soccer, lacrosse and track. After delays stretched renovations for over a year from June 2023, Witter construction finally reached its conclusion on Friday, August 9. Piedmont’s new principal David Yoshihara opened the ceremony by offering thanks, and then handing the microphone to Piedmont School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, board president Veronica Thigpen, Board of Education member Cory Smegal, and Piedmont Boosters representative Keri Elmquist. Piedmont Director of Facilities Pete Palmer received stark criticism for the delays of Witter Field. Keri Elmquist (left), Pete Palmer, and school board president Veronica Thigpen. “As you can imagine, this project has been in the works for a long time. For those who have lived in Piedmont a while, you’ve known that we suffered through seasons where sporting events had to be canceled, or things had to be delayed and there were a lot of problems with the field,” Smegal said during the ceremony. Renovations began on June 6 of last year and were originally forecasted to reach its completion in December 2023, which would’ve allowed both soccer teams to play its seasons at home and permitted the track team to train at Witter. But, without fail, delays emerged continuously. articles.text: McKeegan Autumn is a great time in the East Bay for professional and amateur astronomers, and there’s one place both come together regularly to look up – Chabot Space & Science Center. At 1500 feet in elevation and straddling the border of Alameda and Contra Costa counties, Chabot is the best place possible for an observatory. Since 1883, Chabot has been the Bay Area’s go-to place to learn about and use telescopes. The public has access to three telescopes at Chabot: Leah, an eight-inch refractor telescope, Rachel, a 20-inch refractor telescope (the largest refractor in the Western US regularly open to the public!), and Nellie, a 36-inch reflector telescope. Leah, Rachel, and Nellie welcome the public every Friday and Saturday nights from 7:30 to 10:30 clear weather permitting. Professional and volunteer astronomers and Chabot staff are always on hand to enhance the experience and explain what’s up above. In addition to the regular Friday and Saturday night viewings, Chabot provides access to its telescopes through a wide variety of public events for all ages. Check out its events listings at www. chabotspace.org. In addition to its history as a public resource, Chabot’s telescopes have witnessed and contributed significantly to astronomical and aerospace history. Rachel the telescope assisted in observations and tracking of Apollo spacecraft during the Apollo moon missions in the 1960s and 70s, as part of a network of optical observatories that NASA enlisted. Most famously, observations with Rachel were made of Apollo 13 on its emergency return flight to Earth after the explosion that damaged it, supplying NASA with vital trajectory information to help guide the spacecraft safely through reentry to Earth’s atmosphere. Current research being done at Chabot involves Nellie the telescope in Near Earth Object tracking. Nellie is used to observe and track the motion of asteroids (and sometimes comets) that are classified as Near Earth Objects (NEOs; objects whose orbits can bring them close to Earth’s orbit), and particularly potentially hazardous asteroids: those whose orbits actually cross Earth’s orbit, and so pose a potential risk for impact. If you’ve ever wanted to see what the skies look like through professional telescopes, or want to hang out with other astronomy enthusiasts, check out Chabot Space & Science Center. Ben Burress and Gerald McKeegan are Chabot astronomers. Visitors of all ages and experience levels can explore Bay Area skies through Chabot Space & Science Center’s telescopes.

articles.text: It’s back to school time. A time when parents are taking a deep breath. While summer can be super fun, it can also be exhausting because there is so much less structure to the schedule. So, back to the day to day it is for kids and their anxious parents. Get up, get ready, shoes on, out the door and into the classroom on time and ready to learn, As school begins, it can become easy to think that the year needs to follow a specific path and have one set outcome for kids. Of course, we all want our kids to do well in school. But, the definition of “do well in school” can be looked at from different perspectives. It could be a prescribed concept that means one specific path, or it could be a developing idea that shifts and changes daily. School is all about learning. And, as a parent, we can get stuck in believing that the learning journey has a set outcome goal– get good grades, do the right activities, and eventually, get into the right college. This is typically how we all think about school. Every day is one more step towards a set outcome. Therefore, if on any given day your child is struggling with an element of the school process, that becomes a problem. The steps are predetermined, so the path is already made and the child must follow that path. Or, we can see the day to day of growing up and developing, and therefore school, as a creative process. The creative path doesn’t know its end point. It’s the process itself that creates and reveals the end point. If there is no already-predetermined outcome goal, the child is creating the path every day. All of a sudden, a struggle is not a moment where we are fearful of a bad grade, but instead becomes a gift because an opportunity for learning has presented itself. A child’s passions can lead the way, and if those passions change, that’s ok too because the passions are also determining the path. as a creative process, it allows the child’s experience to formulate the path one day at a time and it releases the parent from stressing about every setback. It’s the process of attending school that creates the endpoint. As a result, each step the child takes, even if it is a tiny step or a sideways step or, even a step backwards, is creating the path and the outcome. articles.text: On Friday, July 19, a group of the Piedmont Seniors went to visit the Rosie the Riveter Museum, which is part of the World War II National Historic Park, located in Richmond. The Seniors were fortunate enough to meet and have a discussion with 98-year-old “Rosie Jeanne” Gibson, one of two remaining “Rosies” who still volunteer at the Museum. “Rosie Jeanne”, who worked during World War II in Seattle, explained about the dire shortage of housing, thus forcing the Rosies to work in shifts around the clock to share the few available beds. During the visit to the museum, a few of the Piedmont Seniors were shown how to make a rivet and gave it a try. The museum has expanded over the years and now includes a third floor devoted to memorabilia and mannequins of workers in the shipyards. World War II when there was a shortage of workers, young women were recruited as riveters and welders. Sometimes it was difficult for the men working in the industry to accept women as equals and there was a reluctance to overcome Depression-era attitudes about women taking jobs away from men. At that time, men often disapproved of married women working at all. The women were critical workers in the war effort, and Richmond became a vital part of the war effort as ships were being made in large numbers at Richmond’s Kaiser yards. After the war, the women were expected to give up their jobs as men returned home from the war. After the visit to the museum, the Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a relaxing lunch at a nearby bistro before heading to the Red Oak Victory Ship built in Richmond in 1944. This ship carried supplies and troops to the Pacific theater of war. For more information see www.ssredoakvictory.com for hours, fees and directions. The Seniors also visited the Rosie the Riveter Memorial, which included the Keel Walk to the water’s edge, including images and memories of the women who worked there. To find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: Names like Gianinni, Ratto, Malatesta and Brignole are prominently displayed everywhere, especially on the important buildings. Levaggi built the first opera house. Soon after this, another opera house was built. Wine vineyards and wine production was everywhere. So were olives and olive oil. The small town was famous for its music festivals and people flocked to all the concerts… enthusiastically of course. Musical entertainment was (and is) popular. The restaurants offered excellent pizza and other Italian specialties. Are we in Italy? No. We are in Sutter Creek, California. Even though the town was founded by a Swiss-German named Sutter, the Italian influence remains strong. The restaurant in Hotel Sutter has a mixed reputation. Everything was superb for dinner on Saturday evening. The prime rib was really prime beef. When we asked our waiter to divide the dinner, he gave us a large portion of prime rib. Each of us got a gigantic “loaded baked potato“ and one of the best salads that I have ever had. The “harvest salad” was beautiful to look at and is easy to make. First, you’ll need to roast some peaches. Mix them with lettuce and some dried fruit and use a raspberry vinaigrette dressing. The price was $20 and was a real value. Our waiter, Aaron, was very attentive and even included a complementary apple crisp for our dessert. When I was beginning my musical career, my teachers always spoke of the great musicians of the past. Friends of mine knew the great composer Puccini and they talked about famous violinists such as Joachim and Sarasate, and many other important Dinner in Sutter Creek personages. In those days, everything was done to let the music speak for itself. Performers on stage were reserved. Buffoonery was for the circus. Sadly, things have changed. In today’s classical world, musicians compete with each other to match the buffoonery of the pop culture. It is important to choose which path you want to go. Last Tuesday I went to one of the noontime concerts at Old St. Mary’s at the vortex of the Financial District and Chinatown. The featured performers were cellist Evan Kahn and pianist Amy Zanrosso. Musically, the concert was a complete delight. As they played, a seamless kaleidoscope of emotions became apparent. The program itself was completely balanced, going from Beethoven to Glazunov and concluding with Benjamin Britten. The musical duo did everything that was necessary. They didn’t need amplification. Evan Khan is the new first cellist of the San Francisco Opera. He is first and foremost an elegant performer. Among his assets are a suave and elegant tone. All of these things were increased because of the immense sensitivity of the pianist, Amy Zanrosso. I don’t think it was possible for the ensemble to be better. Pianist Amy Zanrosso and cellist Evan Kahn presented a memorable concert for San Francisco’s noontime concerts.

articles.text: The de Young Museum, one of the two fine arts museums in San Francisco, is exhibiting impressionist and realist artworks spanning 1848 to 1960 in an exhibition entitled “American Beauty” now through October 20. American art in the 19th and 20th centuries presents a variety of artistic responses during a complex period in US history. Artwork featured is borrowed from Bernard and Barbro Osher, which enhances the de Young’s American art collection with several significant firsts. The exhibition includes the first large-scale oil painting by Winslow Homer (The Angler, ca. 1874), the first genre picture by William Merritt Chase (Spanish Bric-à-Brac Shop, 1883), the first major George Bellows landscape (In Virginia, 1908), the first Georgia O’Keeffe images of the Southwest (Front of Ranchos Church, 1930 and The Patio, 1940), as well as thirteen artists entering the museum’s collection for the first time. To learn more about the exhibition, visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/osher-american-art.

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s new commissioned piece by Stockon-born artist Kara Walker, entitled Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine), is on view through May 2026. Walker is a contemporary painter, silhouettist, printmaker, installation artist, filmmaker, and professor who explores race, gender, sexuality, violence, and identity in her work. She is best known for her room-size tableaux of black cut-paper silhouettes. Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) is a colossal version of her trademark artworks, and marks Walker’s most ambitious large-scale public project to date, as well as the first time the museum commissioned an artist to create a site-specific installation for the Roberts Family Gallery. Walker’s new artwork follows other major exhibitions in the space including Diego Rivera’s Pan American Unity. The commission was organized by Eungie Joo, SFMOMA’s curator and head of contemporary art, who worked with the artists many times over the last 27 years. “Fortuna and the Immortality Garden (Machine) emerges out of the abject loneliness of the COVID-19 pandemic and the ominous depopulation of our once thriving downtown San Francisco,” Joo said. Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA’s Helen and Charles Schwab Director, said Walker’s “profound installation grapples with critical subjects relating to our shared humanity, the rapidly expanding role of technology and our aspirations and fears for the future.” “These topics find fresh life and meaning through the distinct lens of her practice, which has for decades confronted challenging histories and realities through formal experimentation and innovation,” he said. The commission is part of the museum’s vision and mission to present work that has strong resonance for Bay Area communities. “With her towering composition of Black automatons enacting ritual and witness amidst a sea of gleaming obsidian, Walker has created a fantastical space of reflection, memorialization and possibility,” Joo said. “I look forward to spending many hours with the work thinking about our shared future.” To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/fortuna-and-the-immortality-garden-machine/. articles.text: Three artists have combined their talents to present a unique art exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening September 7. Elena Doronkina is an award-winning artist and an American Women Artists associate member. For the last five years, she has been a Program Director at the Alamo Danville Artist’s Society (ADAS) and a manager at Blackhawk Gallery in Danville, CA. Elena’s artistic vision: Fine art, in my opinion, is a vehicle for emotional expression, and I strive to elicit the same feelings in the viewer that I encounter during the artistic process. When the viewer experiences a profound emotional connection, I consider my artwork finalized. Alexander Zimin is an Internationally known Artist from Russia. His first significant exhibition was held in Finland in 1994 (Koscengalleria, Imatra). Since then, he has taken part in more than 60 exhibitions in Russia, the USA, China, Finland, Greece, Estonia, Italy. Prizewinner of the landscape art festival (Carmel, CA) in 2001 and 2002. Teaching: since 2008, Zimin has participated in the international educational project “Repin Institute in Kotka” (Finland), and repeatedly held master classes in painting in California. Natalya Biktairova is a unique modern graphic artist and fashion designer. Natalya has a great sense of color and is a virtuoso in drawing. Art is her passion – her air – and she can’t imagine her life without it. Natalya engages in an interactive process with her clients to select the item that will become the ‘canvas’ for the work and understand the concept that the client imagines.

The commission is part of the museum’s vision and mission to present work that has strong resonance for Bay Area communities. “With her towering composition of Black automatons enacting ritual and witness amidst a sea of gleaming obsidian, Walker has created a fantastical space of reflection, memorialization and possibility,” Joo said. “I look forward to spending many hours with the work thinking about our shared future.” To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/fortuna-and-the-immortality-garden-machine/. His approach is effective for many types of images: forest scenes with overlapping foliage or trees, cityscapes or abstract images with underlying geometric patterns – in short, any image where additional dimensions stimulate closer inspection and the discovery of something that would be missed in a two-dimensional print. articles.text: To watch the work of animator and writer Hayao Miyazaki is to be in the presence of creative genius, a master storyteller who invariably finds that engaging sweet spot: always surprising, perhaps a little scary, and consistently filled with mesmerizing wonder. Made in 1988, My Neighbor Totoro is at the top of the list. If you have yet to sample one of his films Totoro is a solid beginning. The story is absent rough edged villains. There is no conflict, and it is told from the point of view of two young sisters, Mei and Satsuki (Dakota Fanning and Elle Fanning). It is, as well, an extraordinary co-mingling of fantasy and reality, which defines the essence of childhood. Nothing about Totoro is intended to be even remotely spooky. Perhaps touched lightly by sadness, the spare story fits nicely under an umbrella of joy, imagination, and hand-drawn visuals that possess a palate of rich colors and an unfailingly detailed background. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1958. Professor Kusakabe (Tim Daly), a loving father, with his daughters move into an old, creaky house that is filled with enchantment and magic. It sits on the outskirts of a sweeping forest, never forbidding or menacing. The girls immediately take notice of a massive camphor tree that seems to stretch in all directions. The tree, they discover, is the home to a giant, benign creature called a totoro, which can only be described as an amalgam of a penguin, rabbit and owl. The narrative unfolds slowly. We learn that the reason that their father has chosen this particular place to live is that it is close to his wife (Lea Salonga) and the girls’ mother who is in the hospital. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty From the world renowned Japanese Studio Ghibli, The Secret World of Arrietty was co-written by two of its principal storytellers, Hiromasa Yonebayashi and Hayao Miyazaki. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, the Borrowers are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure she finds fascinating by the sheer size of the bean world. She is also drawn into Shawn’s personal world and is soon discovered by the bean boy. Surprisingly these two most disparate characters fashion a friendship and a bond of trust. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Sharon family members Percy Gray painted this watercolor of Casa Montana, the Sharon estate on Mountain Avenue, in the 1920s. The walkers have talked about Frank C. Havens and other early Piedmont real estate developers, but a developer they hadn’t discussed and a street they hadn’t walked this year were William Sharon and Sharon Avenue. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi once devoted an issue of the society’s Piedmont’s History publication to Sharon, his family, and estate. The group decided to walk to Sharon Avenue and discuss its history. The walkers continued to 37 Sharon Avenue where William Sharon’s stories were told. Sharon was born in 1852 and grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he went to San Francisco and then Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, who was a successful banker and silver mine owner. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt in 1876 and they raised a family of 10 children. He became successful in finance and mining and was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. The Sharons initially lived in Virginia City but moved to Oakland in 1890 for better schools. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. In 1897 they hired Frederic D, Voorhess to design their Piedmont home, a magnificent three-story house built in the middle of their property, which they named Casa Montana. In 1914, Piedmont –now an incorporated city – imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property. The Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically, and in 1915 they subdivided their land into a development they called Sharon Terrace. It had 20 lots with frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues, and some family members built homes on them. The driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue, and the address for Casa Montana was changed from 263 Mountain to 37 Sharon Avenue. Sharon died in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home with seven family members and two servants living there. Lillian lived in it until 1934 when she moved to Oakland. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later also built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon, but in 1936 he demolished Casa Montana. The mansion was replaced by three homes at 27, 33, and 37 Sharon. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses remain on the former Casa Montana property, 235 Mountain built in 1908, 56 Sharon built in 1921, and 52 Sharon built in 1922. The walkers took a side trip on Sharon Court. They noted that the exterior 235 Mountain has been updated, and two beautiful red gum eucalyptus trees are in bloom in the front yard. The walkers went up to Pacific, Scenic, and Alta Avenues, with opportunities to enjoy clear views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco. A steep 210-foot set of stairs at 630 Blair got the group back to Pacific, Mountain, Highland, and the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. articles.text: A few months back I wrote about my recent trip to Burgundy. It is an absolutely beautiful wine region and the wines we tasted there were extraordinary. The Pinot Noir and Chardonnay based wines were complex and interesting and I truly enjoyed the trip. Unlike California, French wineries do not charge for tasting – you also do not just drop in you really need to have a reservation. Being a wine writer, I was treated even better than the average visitor and was always shown great hospitality. The problem was when I got home I was struck with the reality that I could not afford to buy the wonderful wines I had been drinking. The cheapest wines I was served start at around 50 bucks and quickly ascend to the hundreds. They were out of my range as they are for most people. The solution to my problem came when I turned my sights a few miles south of Burgundy and began to focus on the region of Beaujolais. The hilly Beaujolais vineyards stretch out from north to south over 55 kilometers, bordered to the west by the foothills of the Massif Central, and to the easy by the Saone River plain. Located just outside Lyon, the Beaujolais region is less than a 30-minute drive away. Unlike Burgundy, however, the red wines of Beaujolais are based on the Gamay grape variety, which reaches its peak here (even though it’s grown around the world). Most Beaujolais wine is red, but white wines produced from Chardonnay and rosés produced from Gamay grapes are also important parts of the region. Still, it’s the red wines crafted from Gamay that are the calling cards of Beaujolais. There are four key red wine categories from Beaujolais: Beaujolais Nouveau, Beaujolais, Beaujolais-Villages, and Beaujolais Cru. They are all from the Beaujolais wine region, but their origins and styles are notably different. Beaujolais Nouveau is a fresh, fruit-forward wine with light (and often barely perceptible) tannins and a more or less straightforward style. The winemaking technique of carbonic maceration, which is most familiarly used for Beaujolais Nouveau, results in the grapes fermenting within their skins, allowing the winemaker to produce a red wine of freshness and vibrancy. Wines labeled Beaujolais are made from grapes grown throughout the Beaujolais region, especially in the south. These also tend to be quite fruit-forward and are meant to be enjoyed early on. Beaujolais-Villages wines are based on Gamay grapes that were grown in the northern part of the Beaujolais region, specifically 38 permitted villages. And Beaujolais Cru — also called Cru Beaujolais — are grown in any of ten specific locales whose typically granitic soils (though they are far from uniform in composition and character) can produce the most age-worthy and complex of all red wines from Beaujolais. Beaujolais also offers a wide range of food-pairing options. Because of the lack of aggressive tannins in Gamay, and the overall character of the red wines of Beaujolais, they tend to work well alongside everything from lighter meats to even fish. articles.text: Photos by Oakland Zoo August 13 Update: He’s been gaining weight steadily, is now six pounds, sleeps well, and is slowly transitioning from kitten milk replacer to solid food. On the morning of Monday, August 5, Oakland Zoo assisted in rescuing a male mountain lion cub from El Dorado County. This is the 27th mountain lion rescue through the Zoo’s Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT) alliance. The cub, which the Zoo has named Briar, was found by residents on a road in El Dorado County. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) conducted ground and wildlife camera surveillance where the kitten was found, hoping to find a mother or siblings to reunite them. However, no other mountain lions were detected on the cameras. After several days the cub was rescued and brought to Oakland Zoo. The Zoo conducted a full examination and determined that he was 4-5 weeks old, making him one of the Zoo’s youngest mountain lion rescues. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital will continue to care for him and monitor him closely as he adapts to human care. Briar will remain at the Zoo until CDFW identifies a permanent home for the cub. Mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother in the wild to learn survival skills. Because Briar is so young, he lacks those skills and cannot return to the wild. The population of mountain lions faces various conservation challenges in the wild, such as habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict, and climate change. Without information about the cub’s mother, CDFW and the Zoo cannot determine how these factors and many other conservation challenges may have contributed to Briar being orphaned. Photos by Oakland Zoo Briar’s name is inspired by the spots on his fur resembling a blackberry bush.

articles.text: – Mark Delventhal He married Laurie Cole at St. Margaret Mary’s Church in Oakland in 1969, and in the same year he and St. Mary’s classmate Rick Tomasco opened Lakeshore Toyhouse. The toy store was immediately popular. Ted was, first and foremost, a people person. He also sold life insurance for a brief time and operated a retail ice cream store in the Fruitvale District of Oakland for Dreyer’s Ice Cream. He became interested in real estate and eventually spent 50 years doing what he loved – holding open houses and meeting people. Initially he bought residential property, fixed them up and resold them, then some years later he became a licensed realtor selling homes in the Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley area. Spectacular sunsets Day five brought clouds and a spectacular sunset over Arrowhead Lake. Adult leader Steve Long had an epic fishing session, catching 40 trout in just over an hour. The Scouts enjoyed playing their favorite card game, “Deuces,” on a granite rock overlooking the lake and Fin Dome. Final campsite and wildlife encounter After clearing Glen Pass, the group found the perfect final campsite at Kearsarge Lakes, surrounded by water on three sides. A young black bear sighting added to the excitement, reminding the Scouts of the importance of proper food storage. Starry Nights and New Games The Scouts learned a new card game from the Cantrills and played late into the night atop a low granite slab at the edge of the lake. Like other nights, they watched shooting stars, the Milky Way and satellites cross the sky before turning in for a wellearned night’s rest. The expedition was a memorable adventure, filled with challenges, achievements and the beauty of the High Sierra. My fitness goals were to increase my vertical, improve my agility and athleticism ,and build more strength. I wanted to be consistent in my training and be as disciplined as possible. How are you measuring your development? I measure my own development by looking back on the previous week to examine where I could improve. An example would be lifting heavier weights and increasing my numbers. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I would occasionally workout with coaches and trainers from basketball, but most of the time I would be on my own. I go to the YMCA to lift and play basketball, but I also frequently workout in a small home gym in our garage. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? In lifting, a recent goal was benching over 200 pounds. In basketball, I would shoot 100 threes from the top of the key, wanting to get 80/100, which I did three times by the end of the summer. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Stay disciplined. You won’t be motivated every day, so maintain a strong work ethic.
